fatal_errors: The proposed W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf composition is not directly supported by the cited evidence as forming a sub-50 nm dual-BCC bulk structure after 40 h milling and sub-1000°C SPS.
Low VEC alone does not establish suppression of brittle intermetallics; VEC primarily informs FCC/BCC tendencies and cannot replace composition-specific phase-stability evidence.

The predicted yield strength is extrapolated from NbMoTaWVTi evidence in which TiO precipitation contributed materially to strength, conflicting with attribution solely to nanograin and solid-solution strengthening.
The falsification experiment does not distinguish grain-boundary strengthening from simple solid-solution strengthening because it lacks grain-size-varied, composition- and phase-matched controls.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the requested general strategy—mechanical alloying followed by SPS, nanocrystalline grains, dual solid solutions, and combined Hall–Petch and solid-solution strengthening—but it is not a reconstruction of the target CoCrFeNiTi processing window or FCC/BCC constitution. The cited NbMoTaWVTi work supports formation of two BCC solutions after 40 h milling and high compressive strength, but SPS produced TiO, and the reported strength was partly attributed to precipitation strengthening. Thus it cannot directly support the claimed oxide-free W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf outcome. Evidence E5 supports milling-driven homogenization and phase evolution, while E1 supports possible thermal stability in a nanocrystalline RHEA, but neither validates the specific composition, sub-50 nm bulk grain size, or asserted 1000°C phase boundary. The proposed temperature and milling-time limits are plausible but largely asserted. XRD, TEM, and compression testing would verify the outcome, while the annealing test probes stability, but these measurements do not isolate Hall–Petch strengthening from solid-solution strengthening. A discriminating test would compare composition- and phase-matched specimens with systematically varied grain sizes, quantify dislocation density, and test whether yield stress scales with inverse square-root grain size after controlling for precipitates and oxygen.
